summary: Extends the procedures for building multicast trees that cross from IP into MPLS regions, using mLDP in the MPLS part, to the case where the link between regions is a VRF table link. It is mainly aimed at uses where VRFs support multicast applications other than multicast VPN.

plainLanguage.summary: A group message needs to travel across two kinds of roads. This document explains how to switch between road types when the link between them is a separate private lane.

questions: multicast across mpls and ip regions
how does multicast cross mpls and ip regions
what is a vrf in multicast
subtitle: How multicast trees cross between IP and MPLS regions when the link between them belongs to a VRF.

tldr.problem: The existing way to convert a PIM multicast tree into an mLDP label switched path assumes the source or rendezvous point is in the global routing table. That breaks when the link between the IP and MPLS regions belongs to a VRF.
tldr.mechanism: The mLDP opaque value is extended to carry the source or RP address, the group address and the Route Distinguisher, so the egress PE can find the right VRF. Four new opaque types cover IPv4 and IPv6 source-specific and bidirectional trees.
tldr.outcome: Providers can carry multicast content for isolated customers or services across an mLDP core using VRFs, one PIM tree per LSP, without full multicast VPN machinery. RFC 7246 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 7438.

today: RFC 7246 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7438. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why VRF In-Band Signaling
sections.content:
A multicast distribution tree may cross both MPLS and non-MPLS regions. It can be built as a pure IP tree with PIM, converted to an MPLS multipoint LSP when it enters an MPLS region (using mLDP), and converted back at the far edge. RFC 6826 defines that conversion, but it assumes the converting routers have routes to the source or rendezvous point address in their global routing tables.

RFC 7246 extends those procedures to the case where the interfaces joining the two regions belong to a VRF as described in RFC 4364. It is mainly aimed at uses where VRFs support multicast applications other than multicast VPN, for example a provider that offers multicast content to customers and uses VRFs to isolate customers and services.

The scope is limited. Only PIM source-specific and bidirectional trees are covered. Source-specific trees always map to point-to-multipoint LSPs and bidirectional trees to multipoint-to-multipoint LSPs. The procedures do not support non-bidirectional Any-Source Multicast groups, do not support cores other than mLDP, and cannot aggregate several PIM trees onto one LSP. For those needs, RFC 6513 and RFC 6514 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already a way to pass a group message from one road onto another. This document adds a way that works when the on-ramp is a private lane with its own rules.

sections.title: Key Terms and Configuration
sections.content:
In PIM, a tree is identified by a source address (or a rendezvous point address for bidirectional trees) and a group address. In mLDP, a tree is identified by a root address and an opaque value. In-band signaling means encoding the (S,G) or (*,G) of the IP tree into the opaque value of the mLDP FEC element. This also helps troubleshooting, since the PIM addresses are visible in the FEC.

Other terms used: RD, the Route Distinguisher that makes a route unique in a VRF context; UMH, the Upstream Multicast Hop, which is the upstream router on the path to the source; and RPA, the rendezvous point address used as the root for a range of groups.

The procedures apply only to groups that are configured for them. Each VRF MUST be configured with a range of multicast group addresses for which mLDP in-band signaling is enabled, and that configuration MUST be present on every PE router attached to sites with senders or receivers for those groups. Other groups MAY use the general multicast VPN procedures, though the VRF is more likely dedicated to in-band signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: Each group message has a sender and a group name. This document copies those two names, plus the private lane's name, into the label system's own form, and only for groups the operator has listed.

sections.title: How a PE Builds the LSP
sections.content:
Suppose a PE router, PE1, gets a PIM Join(S,G) on an interface that belongs to a VRF. Following RFC 6513, it determines the upstream RD, the upstream PE and the UMH for source S. It then sends an mLDP Label Mapping with either a P2MP FEC (for a source-specific tree) or an MP2MP FEC (for a bidirectional tree).

If the UMH and the upstream PE have the same IP address, the FEC root is the upstream PE. The opaque value holds S, G and the upstream RD. For a bidirectional group, S is replaced by the RPA. The Label Mapping goes on PE1's LDP session to the next hop toward the upstream PE.

If they differ, the procedures of RFC 6512 apply. The root becomes the UMH, and the opaque value is itself a recursive FEC whose root is the upstream PE.

When a PE receives such a message and it is itself the root, it uses the RD in the opaque value to pick the VRF. Then, in that VRF, it follows the procedure in RFC 6826 section 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The first router writes down who is sending, which group, and which private lane. The last router reads the lane name, finds that lane and carries on from there.

sections.title: The Four Opaque Value Encodings
sections.content:
Four new opaque value types carry the VRF context. The two source-specific types hold a Source, a Group and an 8-octet RD. The two bidirectional types hold a Mask Len (1 octet), the RP address, the Group and an 8-octet RD.

  • Transit VPNv4 Source TLV: type 250, length 16, with 4-octet IPv4 Source and Group.
  • Transit VPNv6 Source TLV: type 251, length 40, with 16-octet IPv6 Source and Group.
  • Transit VPNv4 Bidir TLV: type 9, length 17, with a 4-octet RP and Group.
  • Transit VPNv6 Bidir TLV: type 10, length 41, with a 16-octet RP and Group.

Mask Len is the number of contiguous one bits, left justified, used as a mask.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four forms to fill in: one for each mix of IPv4 or IPv6 and one-sender or many-sender groups. Every form has a slot for the private lane's name.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The same security considerations apply as for base LDP in RFC 5036 and base mLDP in RFC 6388. In addition, operators MUST configure packet filters so that the mechanism does not cause non-global-scoped IPv6 multicast packets to be tunneled outside their intended scope.

IANA assigned four code points in the registry for the LDP MP Opaque Value Element basic type, defined by RFC 6388: 250, 251, 9 and 10, for the four TLVs above.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual safety rules still apply. Operators must also put up fences so that local-only IPv6 group messages do not escape their area.
